Flagship Dataset of Type 2 Diabetes from the AI-READI Project
Flagship Dataset of Type 2 Diabetes from the AI-READI Project

The AI-READI flagship dataset is a multimodal, AI-ready dataset collected from 2,280 adults aged 40 and older with and without type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), harmonized across three United States data collection sites (University of Alabama at Birmingham, University of California San Diego, and University of Washington). Version 3.0.0 contains data collected between 19 July 2023 and 1 May 2025 spanning survey data, clinical data mapped to the OMOP Common Data Model, 12-lead electrocardiography in WFDB, retinal photography, optical coherence tomography, optical coherence tomography angiography and fluorescence lifetime imaging ophthalmoscopy in DICOM, home environmental sensing, continuous glucose monitoring and wearable activity monitoring. Recruitment sampling aimed at an approximately equal distribution of participants across race/ethnicity, sex and diabetes severity (no diabetes; pre-diabetes or lifestyle-controlled; oral or non-insulin-injectable medication controlled; insulin controlled) so that downstream AI/ML analyses are feasible in ways they are not with claims or electronic health record data. The stated goal is to better understand salutogenesis, the pathway from disease to health, in T2DM. This public version contains no protected health information; information related to the sex and race/ethnicity of participants and medications used has also been removed and is held in a controlled-access version obtainable under a data use agreement.

Organized following the Clinical Dataset Structure (CDS) v0.1.1: one directory per datatype at the root, then one folder per modality, then one folder per device, then one folder per participant named after the participant's study ID number. Per-datatype file format standards are the WaveForm DataBase (WFDB) for cardiac_ecg; the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) Common Data Model for clinical_data, where each CSV file is a one-to-one mapping to an OMOP CDM table; the NASA ASCII File Format Guidelines for Earth Science Data for environment; Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM) for retinal_flio, retinal_oct, retinal_octa and retinal_photography; and Open mHealth for wearable_activity_monitor and wearable_blood_glucose. A separate RO-Crate 1.2-DRAFT metadata package conforming to the FAIRSCAPE profile 0.1 describes the 3.0.0 release and its nine sub-crates.

To enable future generations of artificial intelligence and machine learning research to provide critical insights into type 2 diabetes mellitus, including salutogenic pathways to return to health.

To permit downstream pseudotime manifold analysis, an approach used to predict disease trajectories by collecting and learning from complex, multimodal data from participants with differing disease severity, and so to reconstruct a temporal atlas of T2DM development and reversal towards health.

To establish standards, best practices and guidelines for the collection, preparation and sharing of data for AI/ML purposes, and to serve as a model and blueprint for future data generation projects, following the Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable principles.
The lack of well-designed, high quality, large and inclusive multimodal datasets that are AI ready for training AI models on complex, multi-organ diseases such as T2DM.

The under-representation in past research of racial and ethnic groups that bear a higher burden of disease; a meta-epidemiological review of T2DM studies published from 2000 to 2020 found that samples lacked racial and ethnic diversity.
The infeasibility of downstream AI/ML analyses with existing data sources such as claims or electronic health records data, which the multi-domain acquisition protocol is designed to overcome.
Pseudotime manifold analysis to predict disease trajectories from complex, multimodal data across participants of differing disease severity, from normal to insulin-dependent T2DM.
Development of AI/ML models on a hypothesis-agnostic, multimodal T2DM dataset, using the recommended 70/15/15 training, validation and testing split distributed with the release.

An individual patient. Each instance consists of all of the data available for one individual participating in the study, across survey, clinical, retinal imaging, environmental sensor, continuous glucose monitor and wearable activity monitor modalities.

No labels or targets are provided. The healthsheet records that no specific labeling was performed, as the dataset is hypothesis-agnostic and aimed at facilitating multiple potential downstream AI/ML applications, and that no software was used to label instances.
One or more data modalities for some participants

Some participants elected not to participate in some study elements; in a few cases the data collection device had no stored results or was returned too late to retrieve the results, for example because the battery died or data were lost; in a few cases a data collision occurred at some point in the process and data were lost.

The modalities encompass tabular data, imaging data and physiological signal/waveform data; there is no unstructured text data in the dataset. The first version of the dataset contained 204 instances and the second 1,067 instances.
All instances are part of the same prospective data generation project (AI-READI). There is currently only one visit per participant, so instances are not linked longitudinally in this version.

The release includes a recommended split into training, validation and testing sets in 70%/15%/15% proportions, distributed in the participants.tsv metadata file. Because sex, race and ethnicity are not released with the public version of the dataset, the project team prepared the split so that the validation and test sets are balanced as well as possible for sex, race/ethnicity and diabetes status (no diabetes; pre-diabetes or lifestyle controlled; oral medication controlled; insulin controlled). The split totals 1,576 training, 352 validation and 352 test participants, with a mean age of 60.8 +/- 11.3 years overall. The split is new in version 3.0.0 and is described as aimed at reducing disparities in models developed using this dataset.

In survey data, skipped questions or incomplete responses are expected.

In wearable data, improper use and technical failure such as battery failure or system malfunction are expected. The Garmin activity monitor has gaps in data collection because the battery had to be charged every two to three days.
In imaging data, patient uncooperation, noise that may obscure the images, technical failure such as system malfunction, and data transfer failures are expected.
In a few cases there may have been a data collision at some point in the process, resulting in lost data.

Image quality for the undilated handheld Optomed Aurora fundus camera varies from patient to patient and within the same patient, because obtaining a good view is challenging without dilation and the device is handheld.
selection_bias
Participants are volunteers, so the sample is subject to volunteer bias, which may limit the generalizability of results to those not represented in the study population.
representation_bias

Recruitment is predominantly urban and hospital-based, which may not fully capture all possible cultural and socioeconomic backgrounds, and the cohort does not include other races and ethnicities such as Pacific Islanders and Native Americans.

Three recording sites were strategically selected for geographic variability across the United States and to ensure representation across various racial and ethnic groups, and individuals from all demographic backgrounds were recruited at all three sites.
sampling_bias

Although the cross-sectional database ultimately aims to achieve balance across race/ethnicity, biological sex, and diabetes presence and severity, interim releases are not balanced across these parameters; as enrollment is ongoing, periodic updates to data releases may not have achieved balanced distribution across groups.
The pilot data release and subsequent periodic version releases, including this one.

Uniform data collection protocols were implemented for all subjects irrespective of race/ethnicity, biological sex, or diabetes severity, across all study sites, and the study sites were selected to ensure varied representation and minimize the potential for sampling bias.
selection_bias
Eligibility required participants to speak and read English, which the protocol publication notes may have created challenges in recruiting Hispanic and/or Asian persons.
representativeness_limitation

The study cohort may not provide a comprehensive representation of the population: recruitment is predominantly urban and hospital-based and the cohort excludes races and ethnicities such as Pacific Islanders and Native Americans.
Limits the generalization of models derived from the dataset to populations outside the three recruiting health systems and the four represented racial/ethnic groups.

The full dataset is accessible by entering into a data use agreement.

The study is cross-sectional and there is currently only one visit per participant, so the dataset does not support within-participant longitudinal analysis in this version.

Eligibility restricted enrollment to adults aged 40 to 85 who could read and speak English and provide consent, and excluded pregnancy, gestational diabetes and type 1 diabetes.

No active de-identification was necessary because no identifiers were collected; the team checked that no identifiable data per US HIPAA were present. The public set is stripped of Protected Health Information as defined by the HIPAA Privacy Rule via the "Safe Harbor" method.

Protected Health Information as defined by the HIPAA Privacy Rule (Safe Harbor method) Information related to the sex of participants Information related to the race and ethnicity of participants Medications used

The FAIRhub de-identification level is recorded as deIdentType "NoDeIdentification" with deIdentDirect true and deIdentHIPAA true, and dates, non-arrayed values and k-anonymity flags false. Sex and race/ethnicity were removed from the public set to prevent stigmatization of findings. The RO-Crate records the release as deidentified.

A theoretical risk of future re-identification is acknowledged: AI algorithms can infer individual patient characteristics and could facilitate individual-level identification. To prevent re-identification attempts the project implements a robust data dissemination system, a strict license agreement and data watermarking for both public and controlled sets; the license states that the Data may be statically watermarked to identify the Licensee.
false

Eligibility excluded pregnancy, gestational diabetes and type 1 diabetes, and set a minimum age of 40 years and a maximum of 85 years, so no minors were enrolled. The IRB protocol records that the research will not recruit or obtain data from individuals known to be prisoners, is not likely to have subjects who become prisoners while participating, does not purposefully include fetuses, neonates or pregnant women, and does not include cognitively impaired adults or other adults unable to consent. Native American or non-U.S. indigenous populations are not actively recruited through a tribe or tribe-focused organization.

Separately from this dataset, the funded project committed to engaging in a tribal consultation to address barriers and facilitators of participation, with the goal of collecting similar data within a Native American cohort in an ethical and respectful manner, and the Nature Metabolism comment describes engagement with the Native Biodata Consortium as a co-learning opportunity. These are stated as project activities, not as content of this release.
true

University of Washington IRB protocol STUDY00016228, with initial approval received on 20 December 2022 and an annual renewal application required within 90 days of expiration. Reliance agreements were in place with the IRBs of the University of Alabama at Birmingham and the University of California, San Diego, which used the same consent form with minor institution-specific language.

The RO-Crate names the reviewing body as "Washington University IRB" with the contact given as the IRB Reliance Team, hsdrely@uw.edu, at the Human Subjects Division, University of Washington, 4333 Brooklyn Ave NE Box 359470, Seattle, WA 98195-9470, US. The FAIRhub study description records the human subject review status as "Submitted, approved".

The study is recorded as not FDA-regulated for drugs or for devices, and as having no data monitoring committee. Written informed consent was provided by all participants. Licensees must comply with NIH data security and privacy standards under the Genomic Data Sharing Policy.
Adults aged 40 to 85 years, with and without type 2 diabetes
Pregnancy, gestational diabetes and type 1 diabetes were exclusion criteria
No children, prisoners or adults unable to consent were enrolled
University of Washington Institutional Review Board

Protocol STUDY00016228, initial approval 20 December 2022, with reliance agreements covering the University of Alabama at Birmingham and the University of California, San Diego sites; an annual renewal application about the status and progress of the study is required within 90 days of expiration. The initial approval letter is published with the dataset documentation.

The RO-Crate labels the reviewing organization "Washington University IRB" while giving the University of Washington Human Subjects Division as its address and hsdrely@uw.edu as its contact; the protocol publication and the healthsheet both place the approving IRB at the University of Washington.
AI-READI ethics and bioethics team

The RO-Crate records ethical review by Camille Nebeker, Debra Mathews, Kadija Ferryman and Nicholas Evans. The project states that ethical, legal and social implications are considered at every stage of the project cycle and that guidance from bioethicists informs the standards, best practices and guidelines for collection, preparation and sharing of the data.
AI-READI Community Advisory Board

A Community Advisory Board of 11 persons from the three sites, including diversity in race and ethnicity as represented in the AI-READI sample, contributes to the development of the protocol; the IRB protocol records that the board evaluates the consent forms and research protocols and that its feedback is considered in modifications.
true

Written informed consent, obtained either electronically before the visit (e-consent with an electronic signature through REDCap) or in person at the start of the visit for participants who did not select the electronic option.

The approved consent form for the principal project site, the University of Washington, is published with the dataset documentation; the other clinical sites had IRB reliance and used the same consent form with minor institution-specific language incorporated according to individual institutional requirements. Upon signing, the signed consent form was automatically emailed to the subject, and additional copies could be requested from the study coordinator for the duration of the study.

The FAIRhub consent metadata records the consent type as "ConsentSpecifiedNotElsewhereCategorised" with no non-commercial, geographic, research-type, genetic-only or methods restrictions flagged, and notes that the public version of the dataset can only be used for type 2 diabetes related research while a private version allows more generic use. Consent was required before participation in any part of the protocol, including questionnaires.
Participants were permitted to withdraw consent at any time and cease study participation.

Potential participants were given the option to read all consent documentation electronically before their visit and to give consent with an electronic signature without verbal communication with a clinical research coordinator. Participants could access the e-consent documentation in REDCap and decide at that point not to participate or to request additional information, a call back or a video conference with study staff. No study-specific questionnaires other than the screening questionnaire were available until consent had been given.

Any data that had been shared or used up to the point of withdrawal would stay in the dataset; this is clearly communicated in the consent document. The IRB protocol records that subjects will not be able to withdraw their data or specimens from banking, secondary use or sharing.

Each individual was aware of the data collection, as this was active data collection directly from participants rather than passive collection or secondary use of existing data. Individuals identified from electronic health record screening were mailed a hardcopy invitation letter and sent an invitation email, both personalized to direct them into an online REDCap recruitment interface using links, access codes and QR codes, where they could read an overview of the research program, expectations for participation and answers to frequently asked questions.

The DataCite "Collected" date recorded for this version is the range 2023-07-19/2025-05-01, described as the period when the data was collected; the healthsheet and README repeat this range for the 2,280 participants in version 3.0.0. The overall project timeline spans four years, with one year for protocol development and training and years two to four for subject recruitment and data collection; preliminary pilot enrollment ran from 18 July 2023 to 30 November 2023 and formal data collection began on 1 December 2023. The study start date is recorded as 2023-07-19 (actual) with an anticipated completion date of 2027-01-01.

The protocol publication states that enrollment began on 18 July 2023, one day earlier than the 2023-07-19 study start and collection-period start recorded in the higher-ranked FAIRhub metadata; the FAIRhub value is used here.
true
true

Some data were directly observable, such as laboratory results, vital signs and retinal imaging. Verification of data entry was performed when possible, for example by cross-referencing entered medications with medications that were physically brought in or photographed by each study participant.
true

Other data were reported by subjects, notably survey and questionnaire responses covering demographics, depressive symptoms, diabetes distress and self-care, diet, smoking, alcohol, vaping and marijuana use, general health, social determinants of health, and visual impairment and eye care access.

REDCap was used to collect patient-reported questionnaire data and clinical data recorded at the visit, including the medications assessment, vitals, visual acuity, contrast sensitivity, monofilament test results and complete blood count results. Clinical data outside expected minimum/maximum ranges were flagged in REDCap and appeared in reports viewed by clinical research coordinators and data managers. The exact forms used for data collection in REDCap are published with the dataset documentation.

Philips PageWriter TC30 Cardiograph (Amsterdam, The Netherlands): a 12-lead ECG performed while the participant sits in a reclining chair or lies supine, with the position recorded as 0, 30, 60 or 90 degrees relative to supine. Data are exported in .xml format and distributed under the WFDB standard in cardiac_ecg/ecg_12lead/philips_tc30.

LeeLab Anura environmental sensor, custom designed at the Karalis Johnson Retina Center, University of Washington (Seattle, Washington). Participants were sent home with the device and asked to place it in a frequently used area of the home for 10 continuous days, then to note where it had been placed. It records ambient temperature, relative humidity, nitrogen oxides (NO and NO2), volatile organic compounds, particulate matter counts (PM1.0, PM2.5, PM4 and PM10) and 11 multi-spectral light intensity measurements, exported as .csv.

The device was specifically chosen with participant privacy as a primary concern: it does not capture video or audio, is not equipped with GPS location monitoring and is not synced with participant-owned devices.

Dexcom G6 Continuous Glucose Monitor (Dexcom, Inc., San Diego, California): a real-time integrated continuous glucose monitoring system worn continuously for 10 days that captures blood glucose readings in mg/dL every five minutes without finger sticks. A single sensor is designed to last a maximum of ten days and the transmitter saves data for thirty days, so data must be downloaded within that window. Participants were masked to the results during the monitoring period.

Dexcom provided research discounts on study devices. The IRB protocol additionally permits participants already wearing a Dexcom G6 either to place an additional study sensor or to share their existing Dexcom Clarity data, and offers them the option of allowing download of previously collected glucose values for up to 90 days before the visit, for a total of up to 100 days; the dataset documentation describes the collected CGM data as a 10-day monitoring period.

Garmin Vivosmart 5 physical activity monitor (Garmin Ltd, Schaffhausen, Switzerland). Advised to be worn on the non-dominant wrist for 10 consecutive days, with participants free to choose their preferred wrist, and returned with a form specifying the wrist worn and the dominant hand. The sampling frequency is 5 seconds and the device continuously records physical activity and sleep, including number of steps, heart rate, sleep duration, oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, stress and calories. Data are exported in .FIT format and converted to the Open mHealth standard.

There are gaps in data collection because the battery had to be charged every two to three days. Garmin provided research discounts on study devices. Like the environmental sensor, the tracker was chosen for privacy: it captures no video or audio, has no GPS location monitoring and is not synced with participant-owned devices.

Optomed Aurora IQ handheld fundus camera (Optomed, Oulu, Finland): a non-mydriatic camera with a 50-degree field of view, 5 Mpix sensor and high-contrast optical design, used to take undilated macula- and disc-centered color fundus photographs in a dark room with the participant seated and reclined. Output is DICOM.
Optomed loaned devices for research purposes at no cost.

iCare EIDON widefield TrueColor confocal fundus imaging system (iCare USA, Inc., Raleigh, North Carolina): captures images up to 200 degrees with TrueColor, blue, red, red-free and infrared confocal modalities, operating without dilation at a minimum pupil of 2.5 mm. AI-READI images comprise single field central infrared/fundus autofluorescence and a smart horizontal mosaic, acquired in fully automated mode in a dark room to minimize operator-induced noise. Output is DICOM.
iCare World loaned devices for research purposes at no cost.

Heidelberg Spectralis HRA optical coherence tomography and OCT angiography system (Heidelberg Engineering GmbH, Heidelberg, Germany): combines OCT with retinal angiography using confocal scanning laser ophthalmoscope technology that minimizes the effects of light scatter. AI-READI scans are optic nerve head radial circle high resolution, posterior pole macula high resolution 61 lines, and macula 20x20 high speed 512 lines OCTA, acquired in a dark room. Output is DICOM.
Heidelberg Engineering provided research discounts on study devices.

Heidelberg Fluorescence Lifetime Imaging Ophthalmoscopy (FLIO) (Heidelberg Engineering GmbH, Heidelberg, Germany): a macula-centered, non-invasive measurement of the fluorescence lifetimes of endogenous retinal fluorophores, recorded at short (498-560 nm) and long (560-720 nm) wavelengths and provided as two DICOM files per eye. Exported in .sdt file format and converted to DICOM for the dataset. Because the scan takes longer than a standard OCT and exposes participants to uncomfortable light levels, it is performed last in the visit.

Topcon Maestro2 3D OCT-1 (Topcon Healthcare, Itabashi-ku, Tokyo, Japan): a robotic OCT and color fundus camera capturing 12x9 mm wide-field OCT including macula and optic disc, 6x6 mm 3D macula OCT and 6x6 mm OCTA at a 50 kHz scan rate, acquired automatically in a dark room with minimal operator involvement. Exported in .fda file format and converted to DICOM for the dataset.
Topcon Corporation loaned devices for research purposes at no cost.

Topcon Triton DRI OCT (Topcon Healthcare, Itabashi-ku, Tokyo, Japan): swept-source OCT with a 1,050 nm wavelength light source and a non-mydriatic color fundus camera, visualizing the deepest layers of the eye including through cataracts. AI-READI protocols are 12x12 mm and 6x6 mm OCTA and 12.0x9.0x6.0 mm 3D horizontal and radial scans. Exported in .fda file format and converted to DICOM for the dataset.
Topcon Corporation loaned devices for research purposes at no cost.

Zeiss Cirrus 5000 Angioplex (Carl Zeiss Meditec AG, Jena, Germany): high-definition OCT with non-invasive imaging of retinal microvasculature. Protocols include 512x512 and 200x200 macula and optic nerve head cubes and 6x6 mm macula and disc OCTA, with a 60-degree OCTA widefield view, 8x8 mm single scans and 14x14 mm automated OCTA montage available. Output is DICOM.
Carl Zeiss loaned devices for research purposes at no cost.

In-clinic measurement instruments whose readings were recorded into REDCap: the Montreal Cognitive Assessment administered on an iPad using the MoCA Duo application (MoCA Cognition, Quebec, Canada); the M&S Technologies Electronic Visual Acuity tester (Niles, Illinois) at 4 meters, with a 2.0 neutral density filter or ND-occluder for mesopic testing; the Mars letter contrast sensitivity chart (Mars Perceptrix, Chappaqua, New York) read monocularly under photopic and mesopic conditions with background luminance of 60 to 120 cd/m2; the Topcon KR-800 auto keratometer/refractor; a standard 10 g monofilament applied at three locations on each foot ten times per location with the participant's eyes closed; blood pressure by OMRON HEM 907XL, Medline MDS4001 or Welch Allyn 6000 series monitors, measured twice two minutes apart; and NIDEK LM-600P, Topcon CL-200 or Topcon CL-300 lensometers.
Clinical research coordinators and research assistants at the three sites

Responsible for contacting and consenting research participants, ushering them through the research visit, conducting study visits including collection of ophthalmic images, training participants on study procedures such as continuous glucose monitoring and the fitness tracker, and ensuring the return of all study materials. All research personnel who recruited, enrolled and collected data underwent training by the data manager at the University of Alabama at Birmingham and worked from a detailed Manual of Procedures; a certification process was required of all coordinators, including mandatory institutional compliance training for human subject research and successful administration of all protocol elements to at least three volunteer practice subjects.
Effort was supported by NIH award OT2OD032644 based on the percentage of effort contributed, with salaries aligned to the funding guidelines at each site.
Site data managers

Data managers at each site oversaw the data collection process, reviewed REDCap range-check reports with the coordinators, ingested data into the REDCap database and extracted it for processing, and were responsible for the quality control of all data before uploading to FAIRhub.
Central laboratory

Participants were recruited in waves to facilitate efficient sampling of the study base, with the composition and size of each wave influenced by the observed participation characteristics of race/ethnicity, gender, severity of T2DM and site; composition was monitored and adjusted by under- and oversampling groups as needed. For each wave a contact pool was identified by screening electronic health records at each site for ICD-10 diagnosis codes R73.09 and E11.X, with patients without diabetes identified as those without encounters with these codes. Recruitment aimed at approximately equal proportions of four race/ethnic groups, four categories of T2DM severity and biological males and females, rather than at matching the demographic distribution of the US population. The study is registered with a sampling method of "Non-Probability Sample" and an observational cohort, cross-sectional design.

All patients aged 40 years or older who had a medical encounter within each health system site (University of Alabama at Birmingham, University of California San Diego, University of Washington) between 2020 and 2025.

The cohort is deliberately balanced rather than demographically representative; recruitment is predominantly urban and hospital-based; participants are volunteers; and races and ethnicities such as Pacific Islanders and Native Americans are not included.

The healthsheet states that the dataset contains all possible instances, meaning data from all participants enrolled within the collection period, and answers "N/A" to the question of the sampling strategy used to draw the dataset from a larger set.

Quality control at the time of data entry and acquisition: clinical data outside expected minimum and maximum ranges were flagged in REDCap and visible in reports viewed by clinical research coordinators and data managers, who examined participant records and determined whether an error was likely. Data were checked, and edited where errors were detected, for credibility based on range checks, incorrect flow through prescribed skip patterns, missing data that could be directly filled from other portions of an individual's record, and the omission and/or duplication of records. Editing was done only under the guidance and approval of the site principal investigator; where there was no logical or appropriate way to correct the data, the site principal investigator reviewed the values and decided whether they should be removed.

The data manager at each data site was responsible for the quality control of all data before uploading to FAIRhub, and the dataset was reviewed internally by AI-READI team members for quality checks and to ensure that no personally identifiable information was accidentally included.

After data were sent from each study site to the central project team, all data were mapped to standardized terminologies where possible, notably the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership Common Data Model for observational clinical data and DICOM for medical imaging data, so that the dataset is stored and shared as "AI-ready" and enables immediate AI/ML research without reformatting and preprocessing.

Conversion of proprietary device exports into standard formats: Topcon Maestro2 and Triton data exported in .fda file format and converted to DICOM for the dataset; Heidelberg FLIO data exported in .sdt file format and converted to DICOM; Garmin activity data exported in .FIT file format and converted to the Open mHealth standard; ECG data converted to WFDB; environmental sensor and CGM exports handled as delimited text.

Removal of protected health information from the public release using the HIPAA Safe Harbor method, together with removal of information related to the sex and race/ethnicity of the participants and of medications used.

Montreal Cognitive Assessment administered electronically on an iPad using the MoCA Duo application, capturing all participant responses interactively.

The total possible score is 30, with higher numbers representing better performance; a score below 24 is described as a sign of cognitive impairment and a final total score of 26 and above as normal. Mars letter contrast sensitivity chart read monocularly under photopic conditions with a general occluder and under mesopic conditions with a neutral density occluder, in the standardized order photopic OD, photopic OS, mesopic OD, mesopic OS.

The dataset is distributed to third parties outside the creating entity and is available for public use through the FAIRhub platform. Onward sharing by licensees is tightly bounded: a licensee may not transfer, license, sublicense, sell, assign, display, share or otherwise convey any portion of the Data or any derivative work to any third party other than another licensee bound by an identical agreement, and then only for the purpose of collaborating on one or more projects involving the Data.
AI/ML research on type 2 diabetes mellitus

The multimodal dataset is gathered to facilitate downstream pseudotime manifolds and various applications in artificial intelligence. Use of the public version is restricted by consent and license to type 2 diabetes related research.
Studying salutogenesis, the pathway from disease to health, in T2DM
Multimodal model development across imaging, waveform, wearable and tabular clinical data
Disease trajectory modeling

Data collection was specifically designed to permit downstream pseudotime manifold analysis, an approach used to predict disease trajectories by learning from complex, multimodal data from participants with differing disease severity, ranging from normal to insulin-dependent T2DM, with the long-term objective of reconstructing a temporal atlas of T2DM development and reversal towards health.
Model training, validation and testing using the recommended splits

The recommended 70%/15%/15% split distributed in participants.tsv is intended for subsequent training, validation and testing, with validation and test sets balanced as well as possible for sex, race/ethnicity and diabetes status, and is described as aimed at reducing disparities in models developed using this dataset.
The license forbids making clinical treatment decisions based on the Data, as it is intended solely as a research resource.

The license forbids using or attempting to use the Data, alone or in concert with other information, to compromise or otherwise infringe the confidentiality of information about a Data Subject, to invade or compromise their privacy, to attempt to identify or contact any Data Subject or group of Data Subjects, to extract or extrapolate identifying information, to establish a Data Subject's membership in a particular group of persons, or otherwise to cause harm or injury to any Data Subject.

The license forbids sharing or distributing Data with any third party model vendor or developer for training or development purposes, even where that vendor is party to a Business Associate Agreement with the licensee's institution, where training includes model weight modification and other adjustments to a model's logic or operation. A third party model may be used to analyze the Data only if the vendor is party to such an agreement and the model's interaction with the Data is limited to short-term interaction such as prompting or querying.

The license forbids transferring, licensing, sublicensing, selling, assigning, displaying, sharing or otherwise conveying any portion of the Data or any derivative work to any third party other than another licensee bound by an identical agreement.

The license forbids reproducing Data in papers, articles, presentations, analyses, reports or publications except that small representative samples may be reproduced in up to five images or figures per paper for illustrative purposes only; larger amounts must not be published, posted or otherwise made available via supplemental files, zip archives, code packages or other means, notwithstanding journal or conference requirements.

Access to the public dataset is conditioned on agreeing to use the data only for type 2 diabetes related research; the consent metadata records that the public version can only be used for that purpose, while a private version allows more generic use.
The license forbids taking any action to remove, obscure, alter or mask the static watermarking that may be applied to identify the licensee for security purposes.

The license restricts storage to servers and devices maintained by and located within the licensee's institution or employer, or to cloud or remote storage and backup services that have a HIPAA-approved Business Associate Agreement in place with that institution or employer.

A theoretical risk of future re-identification exists. AI algorithms can infer individual patient characteristics and could facilitate individual-level identification, so the project implements a robust data dissemination system, a strict license agreement and data watermarking for both public and controlled sets, and the license requires licensees who disseminate models trained on the Data to undertake all reasonable efforts to minimize the likelihood that Data can be memorized, derived, reconstructed or reconstituted through the use or construction of those models. Beyond this, the healthsheet states that the creators do not currently anticipate uses of the dataset that could result in unfair treatment or harm.

Because enrollment is ongoing and periodic releases may not have achieved balanced distribution across race/ethnicity, sex and diabetes severity, models developed on this version may reflect residual imbalance; future users should note that the balance targets apply to the completed cohort rather than to this interim release.

Reimbursement of reasonable costs for parking, public transit or rideshare fees related to the study visit. Transportation assistance in the form of rideshare services offered to study participants who endorsed barriers to transporting themselves to study visits.

The IRB protocol notes that participants may incur transport costs that will not be reimbursed if the fees exceed USD 25, and that the same type and amount of compensation would be given to participants invited back for the year 4 follow-up visit.

No identifiers were collected for the shared dataset, and the released data were checked against the HIPAA Safe Harbor criteria; the public set is stripped of protected health information, and information related to the sex and race/ethnicity of participants and medications used has also been removed.

Participant folders are named after the participant's study ID number rather than any identifier Static watermarking of the Data to identify the licensee, which licensees may not remove, obscure, alter or mask A two-tier release, with a public set and a controlled-access set containing the sensitive variables, the latter requiring a data use agreement License prohibitions on re-identification, contact with data subjects, and extraction of identifying information Selection of at-home monitoring devices with participant privacy as a primary concern: the environmental sensor and Garmin fitness tracker capture no video or audio, are not equipped with GPS location monitoring, and are not synced with participant-owned devices Storage restrictions requiring licensee institutional servers or cloud services under a HIPAA-approved Business Associate Agreement
A theoretical risk of future re-identification is acknowledged; AI algorithms can infer individual patient characteristics and could facilitate individual-level identification.

Within the study, identifiers and study data were stored separately with a maintained link between them, under a Risk Level 3 data security plan, with identifiable information kept on encrypted computers or servers or in locked cabinets or rooms with restricted access at all sites and available only to authorized research personnel. The released public dataset carries no such link.

The dataset description records an alternative title, "AI-READI dataset". Several negative findings recorded in the healthsheet are not carried by any structured slot: the dataset has not undergone any formal external audit, although it has been reviewed internally by AI-READI team members for quality checks and to ensure that no personally identifiable information was accidentally included; no data protection impact analysis has been conducted; the dataset had not been used for any tasks at the time of the release; and there is no repository that links to papers or systems that use the dataset. Biospecimens collected in the study - plasma, serum, buffy coats, genomic DNA, PAXgene RNA tubes and peripheral blood mononuclear cells - are banked at the University of Alabama at Birmingham Center for Clinical and Translational Science for future proteomics, metabolomics, genomics, gene expression and immunological studies, and are not part of this dataset; the protocol publication notes that the biorepository holds a finite number of samples and that procedures for reviewing and prioritizing written requests were still to be developed.

Institutional attribution conflicts between tier-1 sources: the FAIRhub API records Washington University in St. Louis (ROR 01yc7t268) as managing organization, lead sponsor and affiliation of the principal investigator, and the license names it as Licensor, while the RO-Crate names the principal investigator as "Aaron Lee, Department of Ophthalmology, University of Washington" and labels the reviewing IRB "Washington University IRB" while giving the University of Washington Human Subjects Division address and hsdrely@uw.edu contact; NIH RePORTER (tier 4) and both publications (tier 3) place the award and the approving IRB at the University of Washington. Both attributions are represented rather than reconciled. Name expansion conflicts: the FAIRhub study description and NIH RePORTER expand AI-READI as "AI Ready and Exploratory Atlas for Diabetes Insights" and "Artificial Intelligence Ready and Exploratory Atlas for Diabetes Insights", while the protocol publication and the Nature Metabolism comment expand it as "Artificial Intelligence Ready and Equitable Atlas for Diabetes Insights"; the healthsheet uses the "Exploratory" form. Collection start date: the FAIRhub metadata gives 2023-07-19 as both the study start and the start of the collected-data range, while the protocol publication states that enrollment began on 18 July 2023; the tier-1 value is used. Target enrollment: the FAIRhub study description records an anticipated enrollment of 4,000 and the protocol publication and Nature comment give 4,000, while the IRB protocol (tier 2) states 4,600 across four groups of 1,000 and NIH RePORTER describes "4,000+ people"; the tier-1 figure of 4,000 is used. Version scope: the v3.0.0 documentation "About" page states that it is associated with a version "which contains data from the participants of the pilot study phase", identical wording to the v2.0.0 page, which conflicts with the tier-1 FAIRhub metadata recording 2,280 participants collected from 19 July 2023 to 1 May 2025; the tier-1 statement is used. Both the healthsheet and the RO-Crate describe version 3.0.0 as covering data "up through the end of the second year of the study", while the changelog table in the README attributes 863 participants to year 2 and 1,213 to year 3; the date range 2023-07-19 to 2025-05-01 is consistent across sources and is used. Size arithmetic: summing the nine datatype directory sizes reported in the dataset structure description gives 3,815,969,360,064 bytes, which is 419,614 bytes less than the stated total of 3,815,969,779,678 bytes; this record states the total as published and notes the difference, which is plausibly attributable to the root-level metadata files but is not accounted for by any source. Summing the nine directory file counts gives 356,334 files, exactly 9 fewer than the stated total of 356,343, matching the nine root-level metadata files enumerated in the same document. The protocol publication states that "T2DM and pre-diabetes are identified by screening electronic health records for ICD-10 diagnosis codes R73.09 and E11.X, respectively"; the code-to-condition mapping implied by "respectively" is reproduced here only as the pair of codes used, without asserting which code identifies which condition. Blood volume is reported as 53 mL in the protocol publication and as approximately 50-60 mL in the IRB protocol; neither figure is carried in this record because biospecimen collection is not part of the dataset.
